value:
Description (up to 2 marks): both stores attract the same number of customers (5,600), but Store A generates 60% more revenue per week (£22,400 vs £14,000). This means Store A earns more revenue from each visitor (2 marks for a developed, data-referenced comparison; 1 mark for noting the revenue difference without development).
Reason (up to 2 marks): possible reasons include Store A selling higher-value or premium products, better-trained staff who upsell effectively, more effective visual merchandising encouraging impulse purchases, or a more affluent local customer base with higher disposable income (2 marks for a developed reason linked to the data; 1 mark for a vague suggestion). [4 marks total]
note: F2: Equal footfall and different revenue establish revenue per visitor, not conversion rate.

expect:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation using all four data points. Online: 35% growth and the shift in customer behaviour are compelling reasons to invest; however, the lower average transaction value (£38 vs £62) means each online sale generates less revenue, and higher satisfaction scores in-store suggest the physical experience is more valued by customers. In-store: despite declining sales (−18%), the higher transaction value and satisfaction scores suggest investing in the store experience (e.g. improved visual merchandising, staff training, loyalty schemes) could reverse the decline and generate more revenue per customer. Substantiated judgement: e.g. the business should adopt a multi-channel strategy, investing in both channels proportionally, because relying solely on online growth risks sacrificing the higher-margin in-store sales; or a clear justified choice of one channel with counter-argument acknowledged.
Secure (5-6 marks): Both sides considered with some data reference; a judgement is made but not fully justified.
Developing (3-4 marks): Mostly one-sided with limited data use.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points, little or no data used. [8 marks]
